<document>
# Reduced Working Time and Productivity: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

*Review of Work and Employment Research. S. Achterberg, N. Iwu, F. Castell and J. Moreno. Review protocol registered before search.*

## Abstract

We systematically reviewed studies of reductions in scheduled working time of at least 10% with pay maintained, reporting a quantitative measure of output. Twenty-three studies (1998–2025; about 41,000 workers) met inclusion criteria. Pooled across studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0), with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4). Study design, the hours measure and the type of work explain much of the heterogeneity: controlled studies found smaller effects (+8.2%) than uncontrolled before–after studies (+18.7%), studies using actual hours found smaller effects (+7.9%) than those using scheduled hours (+16.6%), and per-worker output fell substantially in coverage-bound work (−8.9%) but not in discretionary work (+0.6%). There is evidence of small-study bias; adjusting for it reduces the pooled per-hour estimate to +9.1%. Effects show no sign of decay over time.

## Methods

**Search and inclusion.** We searched four bibliographic databases and two working-paper repositories, and contacted authors of known pilots. Studies were included if they (a) evaluated a reduction in scheduled hours of at least 10% with no reduction in pay; (b) reported output per worker or output per hour, or data from which either could be derived; and (c) had at least 50 workers. We excluded studies reporting only self-rated productivity. Of 412 records screened, 23 studies met the criteria.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome is the change in output per hour, expressed as a log ratio and converted back to a percentage for reporting. Where a study reported both scheduled and actual hours, we used actual hours. The secondary outcome is the change in output per worker. For controlled studies we used the difference relative to the comparison group; for uncontrolled studies, the change from baseline.

**Coding of work type.** Two coders independently classified each study's setting as *discretionary* (output can be produced at any time within a deadline: case processing, professional services, software, back-office work), *coverage-bound* (output depends on staff being present while demand arrives: counters, contact centres, retail floors, care rotas), or *mixed/unclear*. Agreement was high (κ = 0.84); disagreements were resolved by discussion.

**Synthesis.** Random-effects meta-analysis with restricted maximum-likelihood estimation; moderators examined by meta-regression. Small-study effects assessed by funnel plot, Egger's regression test, and trim-and-fill.

## Included studies

Of the 23 studies, 9 had a comparison group (3 randomised, including the Varden County trial; 6 matched or difference-in-differences) and 14 were uncontrolled before–after designs, including the Halden multi-organisation pilot. Eight studies measured actual hours; 15 used scheduled hours only. Thirteen settings were coded discretionary, 7 coverage-bound and 3 mixed or unclear. Only two studies were in manufacturing, both in the mixed category. Follow-up ranged from 3 to 30 months (median 6). Output measures were record-based in 12 studies and manager-reported in 11.

## Results

### Pooled effects

Across all 23 studies, output per hour rose by 13.4% (95% CI 8.1 to 19.0; I² = 81%). Output per worker changed by −1.8% (95% CI −4.9 to +1.4; I² = 74%). The prediction interval for output per hour runs from −4% to +34%, meaning that a new study in an unknown setting could plausibly find anything from a small loss to a very large gain.

### Moderators

**Table 1. Subgroup estimates of the change in output per hour and output per worker**

| Subgroup | k | Output per hour | Output per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| **All studies** | 23 | +13.4% (8.1 to 19.0) | −1.8% (−4.9 to +1.4) |
| Controlled designs | 9 | +8.2% (4.0 to 12.6) | −4.1% (−7.6 to −0.5) |
| Uncontrolled before–after | 14 | +18.7% (11.2 to 26.7) | −0.2% (−4.0 to +3.8) |
| Actual hours measured | 8 | +7.9% (3.6 to 12.4) | −3.9% (−7.8 to +0.1) |
| Scheduled hours only | 15 | +16.6% (9.9 to 23.7) | −0.6% (−4.3 to +3.3) |
| Record-based output | 12 | +9.7% (5.0 to 14.6) | −3.6% (−7.2 to +0.2) |
| Manager-reported output | 11 | +17.8% (10.0 to 26.1) | +0.4% (−3.9 to +4.9) |
| Discretionary work | 13 | +15.1% (8.8 to 21.8) | +0.6% (−2.8 to +4.1) |
| Coverage-bound work | 7 | +6.2% (1.1 to 11.6) | −8.9% (−13.1 to −4.5) |
| Mixed or unclear | 3 | +12.0% (−1.5 to 27.4) | −2.9% (−10.6 to +5.4) |

In a multiple meta-regression including design, hours measure and work type together, all three moderators remained associated with the effect, and together they explained 58% of between-study variance. The design and measurement moderators overlap heavily: 12 of the 14 uncontrolled studies used scheduled hours, and 9 of the 14 used manager-reported output. Our data cannot fully separate them.

The work-type moderator is the clearest for the per-worker outcome. In discretionary work, output per worker was essentially unchanged in pooled estimates; in coverage-bound work, it fell by about 9%, consistent across all seven studies (I² = 22%). The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work was real but too small to compensate for the hours lost.

Note that the discretionary estimate of +15.1% per hour mixes controlled and uncontrolled studies. Restricting to the five controlled discretionary studies, the per-hour estimate is +9.6% (4.8 to 14.6) and the per-worker estimate −2.7% (−6.5 to +1.2).

### Small-study effects

The funnel plot is asymmetric, with small studies reporting larger per-hour gains (Egger's test p = 0.02). Trim-and-fill imputes five missing studies on the left of the funnel and reduces the pooled per-hour estimate from +13.4% to +9.1% (95% CI 3.9 to 14.6). We interpret this as evidence that small, favourable pilots are more likely to be published or publicised than small, unfavourable ones.

### Duration

Four studies reported follow-up beyond 12 months. Their pooled per-hour gain was +14.0% (95% CI 6.2 to 22.4), indistinguishable from the overall estimate. Effects show no sign of decay, and novelty explanations can therefore be set aside.

### Mechanisms

Eleven studies measured fatigue or wellbeing alongside output. Across these, the study-level correlation between the improvement in fatigue scores and the per-hour gain was weak (r = 0.18). Only three studies measured time spent in meetings, and none tested meetings as a mediator under a registered plan; we cannot assess this mechanism. Sick leave fell in all 14 studies that reported it (pooled −31%), and staff turnover fell in all 9 that reported it.

## Discussion

The literature supports a gain in output per hour from reduced working time, but a considerably smaller one than headline pilots suggest. The figure most often quoted, a gain of more than 20%, comes from uncontrolled studies using scheduled hours and manager-reported output; each of those features is associated with larger estimates. Controlled studies, studies measuring actual hours, studies using records, and the bias-adjusted estimate converge on a gain of roughly 8 to 10%.

Whether that gain is "enough" depends on the type of work. In discretionary settings the evidence is compatible with output per worker being maintained or falling slightly; in coverage-bound settings it falls clearly, and maintaining service would require additional staff.

We do not find support for the claim, made in one re-analysis of the Halden pilot, that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact. The controlled and actual-hours subgroups, which avoid the problems that re-analysis identified, still show gains whose confidence intervals exclude zero. Nor do we find support for the claim that reduced hours are sector-general.

## Limitations

Twenty-three studies is a small base for a meta-regression with three correlated moderators. Most studies are short. Only nine are controlled, and the controlled studies are themselves mostly in the public sector. Manufacturing and shift-based production are almost absent. Classification of work type, though reliable between coders, imposes a binary on what is often a mix within a single organisation.

response:
I've read the review and checked its figures. It is the most careful document in this series, and its headline estimate of roughly 8–10% per actual hour is well supported. It also gets the Halden re-analysis right: it rejects both "sector-general" and "entirely artifact". It makes one error of the same kind that it corrects in the re-analysis, only in the opposite direction: the duration analysis treats a question as settled when the evidence leaves it open. There are also a few gaps in method.

## What the review finds

The review covers 23 studies of hour cuts of at least 10% at full pay, about 41,000 workers in total.

- **Pooled result:** output per hour +13.4%, with very high heterogeneity (I² = 81%). Output per worker −1.8%, with a CI that crosses zero.
- **What drives the heterogeneity:**
  - **Weaker designs give bigger effects.** Uncontrolled studies, scheduled-hours measures and manager-reported output all give larger estimates. These features overlap heavily, so their separate contributions can't be fully separated.
  - **Type of work matters.** Coverage-bound work loses about 9% output per worker, and that result is consistent across studies. Discretionary work holds output roughly steady.
- **Small-study bias:** adjusting for it brings the per-hour gain down to +9.1%.
- **Duration:** the four studies with more than 12 months of follow-up show +14.0%. From this the authors conclude there is no decay and set aside novelty as an explanation.
- **Mechanisms:** fatigue improvements correlate only weakly with gains (r = 0.18). Meetings were too rarely measured to assess. Sick leave and turnover fell in every study that reported them.

## Checks

The figures are internally consistent:

- **Confidence intervals.** All are symmetric on the log scale, as they should be for log-ratio pooling. For example, the overall estimate is ±0.048 on the log scale, and the prediction interval of −4% to +34% is ±0.167 around ln(1.134).
- **Subgroup counts.** Each set sums to 23: 9 + 14, 8 + 15, 12 + 11, and 13 + 7 + 3.
- **Implied study mix.** The stated overlaps show that 6 of the 9 controlled studies measured actual hours and 7 of the 9 used record-based output.

## What deserves full weight

- **The ~8–10% estimate.** Controlled studies (+8.2%), actual-hours studies (+7.9%), record-based studies (+9.7%), controlled discretionary studies (+9.6%) and the bias-adjusted estimate (+9.1%) all land in this range.
- **The coverage-bound per-worker loss.** About −9%, with low heterogeneity (I² = 22%) across seven studies. This is the most settled result in the literature.
- **The treatment of Varga & Holm.** The review answers "entirely artifact" with exactly the subgroups that avoid the measurement problems the re-analysis identified.
- **Honest reporting.** The prediction interval and the acknowledged confounding between moderators are reported plainly.

## Where it goes further than the evidence

**1. The duration analysis does not set novelty aside.** This is the same error Varga & Holm made, in reverse. They declared novelty the explanation; the review declares it excluded. Neither has the evidence for that. Four reasons:

- **It compares different studies, not the same studies over time.** It sets four long studies against all the others, rather than following effects within studies. Decay would show up as a declining trajectory within a study.
- **We don't know which four studies these are.** If they are mostly uncontrolled, scheduled-hours designs, the right comparison is the +18.7% of that group, not the +13.4% overall. Against +18.7%, +14.0% could actually indicate decay.
- **Long studies are selected on success.** Organisations that keep a scheme running past 12 months are the ones for which it worked. In Halden, the reverters would never have produced long-run data.
- **The CI is too wide to rule out decay.** At +6.2% to +22.4%, it is compatible with gains shrinking to a third of the pooled figure.

The honest statement is that gains are still present at 12 months or more in the few studies that ran that long, and that whether they decay is open. Within-study trajectories would settle it.

**2. The estimates that agree are not independent.** Because the moderators overlap, the controlled, actual-hours and record-based subgroups are largely the same handful of studies. Their agreement is one finding seen from several angles, not several confirmations.

Two further problems with the adjustments:

- **The corrections are never combined.** The trim-and-fill adjustment is applied to all 23 studies, including the inflated designs, and is not applied to the subset with the strongest designs. The estimate the reader most needs is not reported: studies that are controlled, use actual hours, and use record-based output, ideally restricted to discretionary work. It may well come out below 8%.
- **The small-study adjustment may not mean what the authors say.** Trim-and-fill performs poorly when I² is 81%. Funnel asymmetry may simply reflect that small studies are mostly uncontrolled pilots, rather than publication bias. The +9.1% is a reasonable sensitivity analysis, not a corrected estimate.

**3. There is no risk-of-bias assessment.** A systematic review would normally report one (for example, RoB 2 or ROBINS-I). This series shows why it matters. Halden's published text described its withdrawals as happening during preparation, but the microdata showed they happened during the pilot and were related to how organisations were coping. A review that relies on published reports would miss that unless it assessed attrition explicitly.

**4. It is unclear how two key studies were coded.**

- **Varden.** It reports separate results for discretionary and coverage-bound work, yet it counts as one study among 23, and each study gets a single work-type code. If Varden was coded as mixed, its cleanest contribution, a randomised comparison of the two kinds of work, has been averaged away.
- **Halden.** Did the review use the published +23.4%, or the re-analysis's actual-hours and record-based figures for the subset where they exist? The review's own rule ("where a study reported both… we used actual hours") points toward the corrected figures, but they come from a different paper.

**5. The abstract undersells the per-worker loss.** The abstract gives the pooled per-worker change as −1.8%, with a CI crossing zero. In controlled studies, though, it is **−4.1%, with a CI excluding zero**. For an employer, the per-worker figure is the one that matters, and the better-designed studies find a modest loss.

**6. Two smaller points:**

- **The per-hour gain in coverage-bound work is mostly higher utilisation.** The review calls this +6.2% "real", the same reading I questioned in Varden. With fewer staff on duty, each staff member has less idle time, and the cost moves to customers' waiting time.
- **The fatigue correlation tells us almost nothing.** r = 0.18 across 11 studies has a 95% CI of roughly −0.47 to 0.70. It is no evidence against fatigue as a mechanism, only an absence of evidence either way.

## Updated synthesis across the four documents

Last time I put the per-actual-hour gain in discretionary work at roughly 10–13%. That range rested on two studies: Halden's corrected subset (+10.8%) and Varden's case-processing offices (+12.5%). The broader evidence puts it somewhat lower, at **roughly 8–10%**. The two earlier estimates sit at the upper end of the review's intervals, and both are consistent with it.

| Status | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Settled** | Scheduled hours, manager-reported output and uncontrolled designs each inflate estimates. In coverage-bound work, cutting hours at the same headcount reduces output by about 9% per worker. Sick leave falls, by about 30%. |
| **Supported, provisional** | Output per actual hour rises by about 8–10% in discretionary work. Output per worker in discretionary work falls slightly or stays flat (about −3% in the best-designed studies). |
| **Open** | Whether gains last beyond about 12 months. Whether the gain comes from rest, workflow changes or novelty. The pooled effect in studies that pass every design filter at once. |

I can draft reviewer comments for the authors or a one-page evidence summary for a decision-maker.
